title: Security Testing: SAST, DAST & Fuzzing
summary: The automated techniques for finding vulnerabilities before an attacker does, and where each one actually fits in a CI/CD pipeline.

slides.markdown:
Manual code review, covered in the previous topic, doesn't scale to every line of every commit — automated security testing is what fills that gap. Three techniques dominate: **SAST** (scanning source code without running it), **DAST** (attacking a running instance like an outside attacker would), and **fuzzing** (throwing malformed or random input at code to find crashes).

Each technique sees a genuinely different slice of risk, which means none of them substitutes for the others — a mature pipeline runs multiple, at different stages, and knowing which finds what (and, just as importantly, what each one structurally *cannot* find) is the actual interview-relevant skill here, more than being able to name the tools.

slides.subTitle: Scanning source code for known-bad patterns
slides.markdown:
**Static Application Security Testing (SAST)** analyzes source code — without running it — looking for patterns known to be dangerous: string-concatenated SQL queries, use of a deprecated/insecure crypto function, data from a request flowing into a command execution call without sanitization in between (a **tainted data flow**).

Because it never runs the code, SAST can check every line, every branch, every function — including code paths that are rarely or never exercised by tests, which is a real strength no dynamic technique shares. The trade-off is a real **false-positive rate**: SAST tools flag patterns that are statistically risky but frequently fine in context, and a team that doesn't triage findings (rather than either ignoring the tool entirely or blocking every build on every flag) will either drown in noise or stop trusting the tool within a few weeks.

slides.subTitle: Attacking a running instance like a black box
slides.markdown:
**Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)** tests a running application from the outside, the way an actual attacker would — sending real HTTP requests, malformed inputs, and known attack payloads against live endpoints, with **no access to source code at all**. It's checking observable behavior: does this input trigger an error that leaks a stack trace, does this payload get reflected unescaped in the response, does this endpoint return data it shouldn't for this user.

Because DAST tests the actual deployed system rather than source code in isolation, it catches issues that only exist in the full running stack — a misconfiguration in the web server, an interaction between two components that individually look fine, a missing header — that SAST, which never runs anything, structurally cannot see. The trade-off is coverage depth: DAST can only test what it can actually reach and exercise through the running application's exposed surface, so code paths that are hard to trigger externally (a rarely-hit admin function, a code branch behind a feature flag DAST doesn't know to enable) may go entirely untested.

slides.subTitle: Throwing malformed or random input to find crashes
slides.markdown:
**Fuzzing** feeds a program a very large volume of malformed, random, or systematically mutated input and watches for crashes, hangs, or memory-safety violations — it's not looking for a specific known vulnerability pattern, it's looking for **any input that breaks an assumption the code makes**, which makes it uniquely good at finding vulnerability classes nobody was specifically looking for.

**Coverage-guided fuzzing** (AFL, libFuzzer) is the modern default: the fuzzer instruments the code to see which branches a given input exercised, then deliberately mutates inputs to explore *new* code paths rather than randomly retrying inputs that already hit familiar territory — dramatically more efficient than pure random input generation at finding the rare, deeply-nested code path where a bug is actually hiding.

Fuzzing is the primary technique for finding memory-safety bugs (buffer overflows, use-after-free) in languages like C/C++ that don't prevent them by construction, and for finding parser bugs in anything that processes untrusted, structured input — file formats, network protocols, serialization formats — where a malformed input can trigger behavior the original author never considered.

slides.sectionTitle: Where each technique fits in the pipeline
slides.markdown:
| | SAST | DAST | Fuzzing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runs against | Source code, statically | A live, deployed/running instance | A running program, fed generated input |
| Typical CI stage | On every commit/PR — fast enough to gate merges | Against a staging deployment, often nightly or pre-release — needs a running environment | Often continuous, long-running in the background against critical parsers/libraries |
| Speed | Fast — minutes | Slower — needs a real deployment and live requests | Very slow to find anything, but runs indefinitely in the background |
| Best at | Broad code coverage, tainted-data-flow bugs, known-bad patterns | Real deployment misconfigurations, issues only visible in the running system | Memory-safety bugs, parser bugs, genuinely novel crash-inducing input |

The practical pipeline shape this suggests: SAST on every PR as a fast, cheap gate; DAST against a staging environment before a release, since it needs something real to attack; fuzzing as a continuous background process against the highest-risk components (parsers, anything touching untrusted binary input) rather than a per-commit gate, since it needs sustained runtime to find anything and isn't the kind of check that blocks a merge.

slides.subTitle: Different guarantees
slides.markdown:
| | Automated scanning (SAST/DAST/fuzzing) | Penetration testing |
|---|---|---|
| Who/what performs it | Tools, running continuously or on a schedule | A skilled human (or team), typically periodic | 
| Finds | Known patterns, reachable code paths, crash-inducing input | Business-logic flaws, creative multi-step attack chains, anything requiring human judgment about what "shouldn't" be possible |
| Coverage | Broad but shallow — many checks, limited reasoning depth | Narrow but deep — fewer targets, much more creative and contextual reasoning |
| Cadence | Continuous / every commit | Periodic — often quarterly or before a major release, due to cost and time |

A pentester can chain together three individually-unremarkable findings — a slightly verbose error message, a predictable ID scheme, a missing rate limit — into an actual account-takeover path, which is exactly the kind of creative, multi-step reasoning no automated tool does. Automated scanning and pentesting aren't redundant; they cover a speed/depth trade-off, and a mature security program budgets for both rather than treating either as sufficient alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: SAST false-positive rates in practice
slides.markdown:
It's common for SAST tools, run without tuning against a real codebase, to flag findings where a meaningful share — sometimes the majority, depending on the tool and how aggressively it's configured — turn out to be false positives or low-severity noise on triage. This isn't a defect unique to any one vendor; it's inherent to static analysis reasoning about code without actually running it, which forces the tool to be conservative about what it flags as potentially dangerous.

The practical consequence: a team that turns on SAST and immediately makes every finding a hard build-blocker without any tuning or triage process will either grind development to a halt or, more commonly, get an exception carved out that quietly disables the check entirely within a few sprints. The teams that get lasting value tune severity thresholds, suppress known-false-positive patterns explicitly (with a comment explaining why, not silently), and treat only high-confidence, high-severity findings as build-blocking — everything else routes to a reviewed backlog instead of an all-or-nothing gate.

slides.sectionTitle: Choosing where to invest given limited security engineering time
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
A staff-level answer doesn't just describe all three techniques — it reasons about where a limited security engineering budget actually pays off for a *specific* system, because the three techniques aren't equally valuable for every codebase. A typical CRUD web application, mostly business logic and database access with no memory-unsafe code and little untrusted binary parsing, gets most of its value from SAST (broad, cheap coverage of common web vulnerability patterns) and DAST (catching real deployment issues) — fuzzing has comparatively little to find there, because there's little memory-unsafe or complex-parsing surface for it to exercise.

Conversely, a component that parses untrusted binary formats — a media processing library, a custom network protocol implementation, anything written in C/C++ handling attacker-controlled bytes — is exactly where fuzzing finds bugs that SAST and DAST routinely miss, because the vulnerability class (memory corruption from a specific malformed byte sequence) isn't a recognizable static pattern and isn't reachable through a normal DAST-style HTTP attack surface.

The interview-relevant judgment: naming which technique to prioritize *for a given system's actual risk profile*, rather than reciting "use all three everywhere," is what separates a genuinely senior answer from a checklist recitation.

slides.sectionTitle: Why continuous testing beats a one-time audit
slides.markdown:
A one-time security audit — SAST, DAST, and a pentest run once before a major launch — gives a snapshot of the system's security posture *at that moment*. Every commit after that snapshot is unverified by any of it, and code changes fast enough that the snapshot's relevance decays quickly, sometimes within weeks.

This is the argument for **continuous, automated testing integrated into the pipeline itself** rather than periodic point-in-time audits as the primary mechanism: SAST on every PR catches a new vulnerable pattern the moment it's introduced, not months later during the next scheduled audit; DAST against every staging deploy catches a new deployment misconfiguration before it reaches production, not after an attacker finds it. Periodic deep techniques — pentesting, in particular — remain valuable specifically for what continuous automation can't do (creative, multi-step human reasoning), but they're a complement to continuous automated testing, not a substitute for it, and treating an annual pentest as "we did our security testing for the year" leaves eleven months of unverified changes in between.

slides.sectionTitle: Treating a clean SAST scan as proof the code is secure
slides.markdown:
The pitfall: a SAST scan runs clean — no findings — and the team concludes the code is secure, when a clean SAST result only means "no pattern this specific tool was configured to recognize was found in the source code it analyzed." It says nothing about business-logic flaws (a workflow that's exploitable in a way no static pattern captures), nothing about deployment-time misconfigurations (which SAST never sees, since it doesn't run anything), and nothing about vulnerability classes the tool simply isn't designed to detect.

This mirrors the earlier pitfall about SCA scans covered in dependency hygiene: a clean automated scan of any kind is evidence of the absence of what that specific tool checks for, never evidence of the absence of vulnerabilities in general. Combining it with the wrong mental model — "we ran a security tool and it passed, so we're covered" — is how teams end up confidently shipping something a five-minute manual review or a competent pentester would have caught immediately.

The fix is calibrating confidence to what was actually tested: state explicitly what each technique in your pipeline does and doesn't cover, and treat a clean automated result as one input among several (code review, periodic pentesting, threat modeling for new trust boundaries) rather than a final verdict on its own.
